question: What is the main reason we use X-rays and scans in bone and muscle nursing?

options.A: To visualize bone, joints, and soft tissues for diagnosis and monitoring
options.B: To administer direct chemical treatment into the bone marrow
options.C: To replace physical assessment and hands-on patient evaluation
options.D: To permanently destroy damaged musculoskeletal cells and tissues

explanation: Think of imaging as giving us a peek inside! It helps nurses and doctors spot fractures, joint damage, and soft tissue injuries without needing surgery. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T5#GNS222_U1_T5_h1)

question: Why do nurses need to understand how different imaging tests work?

options.A: To operate the heavy imaging machinery during off-peak night shifts
options.B: To independently prescribe the exact type of scan a patient needs in an emergency
options.C: To safely coordinate studies, prepare patients, and guide nursing care based on results
options.D: To replace the radiologist in reading detailed cross-sectional scans

explanation: You won't be running the big scanner machines yourself, but knowing how each test works helps you prep your patient and understand what the results mean for their care! [learn more](GNS222_U1_T5#GNS222_U1_T5_h1)

question: On a standard X-ray picture, why do healthy bones show up as bright white?

options.A: Soft tissues completely block all light while bone lets light pass through
options.B: Bones naturally emit a bright fluorescent light when exposed to air
options.C: The radiologist manually paints the bone structures white after the scan
options.D: Dense structures like cortical bone absorb most of the X-ray beams

explanation: Because bones are dense, they block the X-ray beams from passing through to the film. That blockage is what creates that classic bright white look! [learn more](GNS222_U1_T5#GNS222_U1_T5_h2)

question: A patient asks why they need a special DEXA scan instead of a normal X-ray to check for weak bones. What is your best response?

options.A: Regular X-rays use too much radiation compared to modern bone density scanners
options.B: Standard X-rays cannot detect early bone loss until a large amount of mass is already gone
options.C: DEXA scans take pictures of soft muscle tissue rather than hard skeletal bone
options.D: Standard X-rays are only used for broken bones and cannot look at the spine

explanation: Regular X-rays are great for breaks, but they aren't sensitive enough to catch early osteoporosis. DEXA is specifically designed to measure tiny drops in bone strength. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T5#GNS222_U1_T5_h2)

question: What type of energy does an MRI machine use to take pictures of inside the body?

options.B: Powerful magnetic fields and radio waves

explanation: No radiation here! MRIs use massive magnets and radio waves to create super detailed pictures of your soft tissues and joints. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T5#GNS222_U1_T5_h3)

question: Your patient is scheduled for an MRI, but mentions they have a permanent heart pacemaker. What should you do right away?

options.A: Wrap the patient's chest in a lead apron to block the magnetic field
options.B: Administer a mild sedative to calm the patient before the scan starts
options.C: Proceed with the scan because pacemakers are safe inside the magnet
options.D: Notify the ordering physician and the radiology department immediately

explanation: Hold on! That giant magnet can pull on metal implants and ruin a pacemaker. Always flag this to the team immediately to keep the patient safe. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T5#GNS222_U1_T5_h3)

question: How is a nuclear medicine bone scan different from a regular X-ray?

options.A: It uses sound waves to check blood flow inside the bone marrow
options.B: It evaluates metabolic and physiological bone activity rather than just structure
options.C: It measures the exact length and width of long bones in growing children
options.D: It provides a clear picture of soft cartilage and torn knee ligaments

explanation: While an X-ray just shows the shape of the bone, a bone scan shows what's happening *inside*—like where bones are healing or fighting infection. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T5#GNS222_U1_T5_h4)

question: Why is it so important to encourage a patient to drink lots of fluids after a bone scan?

options.A: To prevent severe dehydration caused by the strong magnetic fields
options.B: To replace the fluid lost during the mandatory fasting period before the test
options.C: To activate the chemical tracer so it can take clearer pictures of the spine
options.D: To help flush the remaining radioactive tracer out of the body through urine

explanation: Drinking plenty of water helps the kidneys wash out any leftover radioactive tracer quickly, lowering radiation exposure. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T5#GNS222_U1_T5_h4)

question: Which lab results must you check before a patient gets IV contrast dye for a CT scan?

options.A: Serum creatinine and blood urea nitrogen
options.D: White blood cell count and platelet level

explanation: Contrast dye is filtered by the kidneys. Checking kidney function tests like creatinine and BUN ensures the kidneys can safely handle the dye! [learn more](GNS222_U1_T5#GNS222_U1_T5_h5)

question: Why is checking pregnancy status an absolute must before sending a female patient for an X-ray or CT scan?

options.A: The heavy lead aprons used during scans are dangerous for expecting mothers
options.B: Contrast dye automatically induces premature labor in pregnant women
options.C: Pregnancy hormones interfere with the machine's ability to focus the beam
options.D: Ionizing radiation can cause developmental harm to a rapidly growing fetus

explanation: Growing babies are extra sensitive to radiation. Always screen female patients of childbearing age to protect an unborn child from accidental exposure. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T5#GNS222_U1_T5_h5)

question: In radiation safety, what does the golden rule acronym 'ALARA' stand for?
explanation: ALARA is a core safety mindset in healthcare: keep radiation doses As Low As Reasonably Achievable using shields, distance, and time. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T5#GNS222_U1_T5_h6)

question: Why is it so crucial that a patient stays completely still during a spine CT scan?

options.A: Sudden movement triggers an emergency shutdown of the X-ray tube
options.B: Patient motion alters the chemical makeup of the radioactive dye
options.C: Body movement creates motion artifact that blurs the images and impairs diagnosis
options.D: Moving too fast can damage the sensitive internal rotating glass detectors

explanation: Even a tiny wiggle can blur the images (we call this 'motion artifact'), making it hard for the doctor to spot a fracture or issue. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T5#GNS222_U1_T5_h6)

question: What is a key nursing check to perform after a patient receives IV contrast dye?

options.A: Measuring hourly urine output to confirm total bladder atrophy
options.B: Monitoring for delayed allergic reactions like rash, itching, or breathing difficulty
options.C: Checking for immediate loss of hair color around the injection site
options.D: Assessing for sudden paralysis in the lower extremities

explanation: Allergic reactions to contrast dye can sometimes pop up hours later. Always keep an eye out for hives, itching, or any trouble breathing. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T5#GNS222_U1_T5_h7)

question: A patient who received a light sedative for a joint scan is awake and asking to go home. What must you confirm before discharge?

options.A: That all physical pain in the joint has completely disappeared
options.B: That the patient has successfully voided a large amount of radioactive urine
options.C: That the radiologist has already completed the final written diagnostic report
options.D: That the patient has stable vital signs, a clear airway, and a responsible escort home

explanation: Sedatives can mess with a person's reflexes and clear thinking for hours. Always make sure they have stable vitals and a trusted adult to take them home safely. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T5#GNS222_U1_T5_h7)

question: Why should a nurse always look at imaging results alongside their own physical assessment of the patient?

options.A: To correlate what is seen on the scan with the patient's actual clinical symptoms
options.B: To legally rewrite the official radiology report if a mistake was made
options.C: To decide whether the patient needs surgery without consulting a doctor
options.D: To replace the radiologist's formal interpretation with nursing judgment

explanation: Pictures don't tell the whole story! Combining scan results with what the patient is actually feeling (like pain or swelling) helps you provide top-notch care. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T5#GNS222_U1_T5_h8)

question: You check a preliminary scan report on a confused patient and discover an unexpected fracture. What is your best next step?

options.A: Notify the primary care provider or medical team immediately for follow-up orders
options.B: Place the patient in strict isolation to prevent further bone damage
options.C: Discharge the patient quickly before the family sees the report
options.D: Wait until the patient complains of severe pain before telling anyone

explanation: Quick communication is key! Letting the medical team know right away ensures the patient gets proper care and treatment for that surprise injury. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T5#GNS222_U1_T5_h8)
